U-S-0001-05-SR-01 (50-50): Speaker 01 introduces the topic of long-term incremental transcript processing, which involves processing the transcript in sequential parts.
U-S-0001-05-SR-02 (51-54): The team discussed whether to conduct experiments on different transcript processing trade-offs (fixed-cut vs. iterative merge), but decided to postpone them until after May 12th due to an impending report deadline. They will proceed by assuming the current implementation is effective without formal proof for now.
U-S-0001-05-SR-03 (55-56): Speaker 01 posits that the current incremental method is advantageous because it filters out irrelevant chit-chat. Speaker 02 attempts to clarify, mentioning a 'forward scan', but then decides to wait for a full explanation of the process.
U-S-0001-05-SR-04 (57-58): The system's core logic involves `retranscript` (reading transcript lines) and `update_issue`. It uses a two-tiered structure of 'Objects' and more granular 'Issues'. An Issue is a tool for tracking recurring topics; when an Issue is mentioned repeatedly, the importance of its associated Object increases. An Object can be linked to multiple Issues.
U-S-0001-05-SR-05 (59-59): The `create_object` function operates by first creating a 'candidate' object. As it reads subsequent text, it merges related content into this candidate.
U-S-0001-05-SR-06 (60-65): The system processes the transcript in fixed chunks of approximately 20 lines. This number was not systematically determined but was an arbitrary initial value that was kept because its performance was acceptable. The window size is not dynamic.
U-S-0001-05-SR-07 (66-66): A previously discussed but unimplemented idea was to use a dynamic analysis window. The system would predict a topic's length (e.g., short for a quick comment, long for a major discussion point) and adjust the number of lines it processes as a single block accordingly.
U-S-0001-05-SR-08 (67-67): A counter-argument was made that the fixed read-chunk size (e.g., 20 lines) is not a limitation, as the system is capable of identifying and separating multiple distinct objects of varying lengths within that single chunk. The object structuring logic is considered more important than the chunk size.
U-S-0001-05-SR-09 (68-69): The verbal explanation of the object structure was insufficient, leading to a request to review the code directly to understand its processing logic, prompting a screen share.
U-S-0070-C01-01 (70-72): An LLM can process a text chunk containing multiple objects/ideas simultaneously. It will identify and store all of them, so there is no need to worry about truncation causing data loss or to strictly feed it one object at a time.
